Hi all,

As I am updating a lot of r-cran-* packages, I am taking the opportunity to
update their descriptions.  After all, if it changed on CRAN, maybe we are
doing a disservice by using the old text with new package versions in Debian.

But then I remembered: in Debian, each time we change a description, there are
dozens of translators who get a notification to review the change and update
their work.  An the descriptions of CRAN packages are very technical.

As of today there are no logistics to contribute back the translations to the
authors of CRAN packages.

Most of the r-cran-* packages are consumed as parts of a dependency chain, and
not installed manually.  Moreover, judging from my own experience, the trigger
for installing a new CRAN package usually comes from reading information
available from the internet, not by screening the Apt cache.

Therefore I propose that we simplify the description of most r-cran-* and
r-bioc-* packages to something like:

Description: CRAN package 'foo' redistributed in Debian.
 The Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) is a package repository for the R
 programming language.  This package was automatically generated for the needs
 of the dependency chain of other Debian packages.  For more information, please
 refer to the upstream homepage or the DESCRIPTION file in
 /usr//lib/R/site-library/<packagename>.

What do you think about it ?

Charles

Hi Dirk,

Here is the code that I used.  It is low quality and ends more like a
scratch space than a real script.  Please feel free to ask me to improve
it before you take more time reading it.  But if you spot bugs I would
be very grateful to hear about them!

https://salsa.debian.org/r-pkg-team/maintenance-utilities/-/blob/be533de817771558160865103d4aef7e3158acf6/rdeps.R

The parsing of the dependency graph is fully recursive including
Suggests, which in the Debian package are generated from the DESCRIPTION
file.  This is necessary because a package in Suggests may be necessary
to run the package's test suite, which is what we run in the Debian
package's autopkgtests.  But obviously the impact on the dependency
graph is strong.

For instance, arch-restricting anything that r-cran-testthat
transitively depends or build-depends on triggers the need to
arch-restrict every package using r-cran-testthat in its test suite,
because we run autopkgtests for every package that provide a test suite.
(Because it allows us to quality control loong64, ppc64el and riscv64,
which we support but on which CRAN/Bioconductor and many of their
upstreams do not run test).

I am not sure if that is the case for r-cran-utf8, but I hope that it
makes the point that the dependency hairball becomes large very
quickly…

Have a nice day,

Charles

Hi Dirk,

I understand your point of view, but autopkgtest's debian/tests/control
only allows to specify Depends (to the best of my knowledge).

The whole point of the autopkgtests (and of enduring the pain they give)
is to search for regressions as extensively as we can, so we take the
broad approach that turns conditional tests into autopkgtest hard
dependencies. (We actually turn all DESCRIPTION Suggests into
autopkgtest dependencies, which know will also include packages not used
by the test suite, because we do not yet have a reliable way to parse
the test suite and deduce its dependencies; please let me know if there
is a standard procedure for this).

This said, I went to the ftp.debian.org mirror and checked the `dak rm`
simulation for the packages listed as the cause for autoremovals of your
packages, and indeed, it is very easy to remove r-cran-utf8 on armel
armhf i386 and s390x.  I am sorry that I did not pay attention earlier.
I have filled #1130603 for r-cran-utf8, #1130604 for r-cran-isoband, and
#1130608 for r-cran-jpeg.

Unfortunately, the dak dependency chain of r-cran-jsonlite,
r-cran-igraph and r-cran-fs are much bigger and contains Bioconductor
packages (see below).  I arch-restricted 165 out of 193 of them today
(DELAYED/2).  The others could not be processed automatically for
various reasons (including failing autopkgtest…).

Next week I will figure out how to check that everything that dak rm
proposes to remove is arch-restricted, make uploads for the packages
that need, and fill the other bugs, unless Paul gives me other
instructions.
 
Have a nice week-end,

Charles

architecture qualifier, but that feels a PITA and just busywork (which

I asked for advice on debian-devel about bulk removal bugs.

https://lists.debian.org/debian-devel/2025/12/msg00106.html

I think that point-to-point replies deviate us from the core of the
discussion.

In any case, I have finished the bulk updates that were automatable,
wich was more than 500 packages.  They will be all out of the delayed
queue by the end of the week-end.   How I reached that point is now a
thing of the past; we had misunderstandings but I think that we can
overcome and eventually forget them.  I understand that people are
frustrated on how long it took but I have a full-time job and a family.

I will follow up with requests for removal and targeted uploads.

Soon, most of the r-cran and all of the r-bioc packages will be
available only on 64-bit little-endian architectures, which is still
broader than what upstream supports.  People aiming seriously at
supporting scientific computation with R and Debian packages on other
architectures should engage with the R community first.  On my side, I
will not upload anymore packages where we turn off autopkgtests on
specific architectures in order to hide the fact that they perform
incorrect computations.

Dirk, I think that we can give you the ownership of the packages that
you need if you prefer not drop architectures in your packages that
depend on ours.  I am also fine for making case-by-case exceptions in
the architecture restricions when there is a serious need.

Lastly, porters who would like to assess the feasibility of supporting
r-cran/bioc packages on their architectures can make local builds and
autopkgtests in environments that provides architecture-is-64-bit and
architecture-is-little-endian.  I am fine with extending the list of
architecures we support if the porters show that they can provide
patches that the R community is willing to accept.

Cheers,

Charles

I do not work at IBM, but look after the R package here, and have also been
somewhat involved in the R Project over a few decades (and am also an R
Foundation Board member ar large).  One of my different activities involved
several runs at building a system for converting all/most of CRAN into .deb
packages with attempts spanning a few decades. (The first one was a neat
Google Summer of Code variant that covered a few thousand packages. Another
one spawned a fairly complete and larger set Don Armstrong did as part of
grad school / postdoc life, I think got high single digit thousands. Both
were outside of Debian proper as we cannot 'flood' the incoming review queue
with thousands of packages. Both died of disk failures and lack of full
backups).

The last attempt I made a few years worked out rather well and is still
ongoing [0] and seeing decent demand coming up on 70 million packages shipped
(I have access to the server logs at the main machine at illinois.edu). For
technical reasons valid at the time I started it, is based on Ubuntu LTS and
covers all/most [1] of CRAN for several current LTS releases. I am right now
in the process of building the binaries for Ubuntu 26.04. I do all of this
via GitHub Actions (as I have no 'bulk' cpu access elsewhere -- though it is
not "that" heavy, I used to use my local server).

I would be happy to chat with you off-line about you starting from my setup
(all at GitHub) to spawn a s390 variant. "It should just work."  The
BioConductor folks took inspiration too and now do the same (though mostly
for use inside Docker).  Maybe we even get to Debian testing on amd64 and
arm64 (two platforms I cover for Ubuntu).

Long story short: this all works, and works well because CRAN pays close
attention to systems and develops / checks quite a bit on Debian testing (in
Vienna) and current Fedora (in Oxford).  So if one takes _consistent_
snapshots -- and I tend to rebuild multiple times daily -- then the
"everything works at CRAN 'at @HEAD'" guarantee is quite useful.  

Cheers, Dirk

CCing Frank, who just posted a similar question on debian-devel.

Thanks Pranav and Frank for your care about R on s390x and
thanks Dirk for the detailed answer,

As Dirk noted, most CRAN packages build fine, and the tools he developed make
it straightforward to build and test them outside Debian. CRAN itself only
tests on Windows, macOS, and amd64 Linux, so on architectures they do not
cover, a clean build does not guarantee correct behaviour. In Debian we have
repeatedly seen a small number of R packages fail their test suites on
non‑64‑bit and non‑little‑endian architectures due to portability issues,
reproducibility problems, or plain bugs.

Because we could not both keep the collection up to date and handle the porting
workload, we eventually had to exclude those architectures. I also expect the
removal of 32‑bit architectures to be permanent unless there is a clear need
for them beyond 2030 (the end of Trixie’s LTS). Debian patches often disrupt
automated upstream‑version updates, and with a large package set maintained
under near burn‑out conditions, the extra porting burden is simply not
sustainable.

This is why most of the current Debian “failures” are intentional: the affected
packages declare architecture-is-little-endian to block big‑endian builds. Once
you have demonstrated successful s390x builds and test runs, and upstream fixes
have been accepted, I will gladly remove that artificial restriction.

Have a nice day,

Le Tue, Mar 24, 2026 at 02:04:44PM +0000, Pranav P a écrit :
> Hi Charles,

> What would you suggest me to do?

Hi Pranav,

First, I recommend reaching out to Frank (cc’d), as he has expressed similar
interests on a different mailing list. Joining forces may increase the
likelihood of success for your project.

I assume you have received—or will soon receive—excellent guidance from Dirk on
automating package builds. The main point I would add is that, to identify as
many s390x-specific (or more generally, big-endian–specific) issues as possible
in CRAN, you should aim to run as many package regression tests as you can.

As Dirk recently explained on this list, some tests are executed conditionally
based on the availability of their dependencies in the test environment.
Ensuring that these dependencies are present is key to making your screening as
effective as possible. The simplest approach I know is to install all packages
listed in the Suggests field of each package’s DESCRIPTION file before running
the tests. This may occasionally result in installing more than strictly
necessary, but for the purpose of bug screening, this is perfectly acceptable.

I am not fully familiar with how CRAN or upstream projects run package tests.
In Debian, however, we aim to run all scripts found in a package’s tests
directory using the autopkgtest framework. You do not need to follow this
system exactly, but feel free to ask if you would like more details about how
it works. One recurring bottleneck to automation, in my experience, is the
variable quality of test suites: in some cases, the contents of the tests
directory do not appear to be designed for continuous integration environments.

Once bugs are identified, forwarding fixes upstream is an excellent way to
build relationships with the R community. You may also uncover recurring
patterns that are of broader interest to R developers. Ultimately, this should
make it much easier to reintroduce s390x (and likely big-endian architectures
more generally) into the set of architectures for which we build r-cran-* and
r-bioc-* packages in Debian, while also fostering shared knowledge, practical
experience, and community buy-in for handling new issues as they arise.

Charles
